goals.title: Describe the celestial sphere model
goals.description: Student can describe the sky as a sphere centered on the observer, and name the celestial poles, the celestial equator, the horizon and the zenith.
goals.hook: Find your way around the sky the way navigators have for thousands of years.

goals.title: Explain why stars rise and set
goals.description: Student can explain the daily motion of the Sun and stars as the result of Earth's rotation, and predict which stars never set from a given latitude.
goals.hook: Know why the sky turns every night, and which stars you will always see.

goals.title: Estimate angles on the sky
goals.description: Student can estimate angular sizes and separations on the sky in degrees using an outstretched hand, and convert between degrees, arcminutes and arcseconds.
goals.hook: Measure the sky with nothing but your hand.

goals.title: Explain the cause of lunar phases
goals.description: Student can explain the Moon's phases from the changing angle between the Sun, the Moon and Earth, and rule out Earth's shadow as the cause.
goals.hook: Replace the most common wrong idea about the Moon with the right one.

goals.title: State the conditions for an eclipse
goals.description: Student can state when a solar or lunar eclipse can happen, using the Moon's phase and the tilt of its orbit, and explain why eclipses do not happen every month.
goals.hook: Predict eclipses instead of waiting to hear about them.

goals.title: Explain why there are two tides a day
goals.description: Student can explain the two daily high tides from the difference in the Moon's gravitational pull across Earth, and say why spring tides happen at new and full moon.
goals.hook: See the Moon's pull at the beach, twice a day.

goals.title: Explain the seasons from axial tilt
goals.description: Student can explain the seasons from the tilt of Earth's axis (the angle of sunlight and the length of the day) and rule out the changing Earth-Sun distance as the cause.
goals.hook: Answer the question most graduates get wrong on camera.

goals.title: Identify solstices and equinoxes
goals.description: Student can identify the solstices and equinoxes on a diagram of Earth's orbit and state the Sun's position and the length of the day at each.
goals.hook: Know what the longest and shortest days really mark.

goals.title: Predict the Sun's path by season
goals.description: Student can predict where the Sun rises and sets and how high it climbs at noon on a given date and latitude.

slide_anchor.title: The Sun's Path Across the Sky

book_anchor.title: The Sun's Path Across the Sky

goals.hook: Plan a garden, a photo or a solar panel by the Sun's path.

goals.title: Order the electromagnetic spectrum
goals.description: Student can order the bands of the electromagnetic spectrum by wavelength, frequency and photon energy, and relate wavelength to color.
goals.hook: Read the universe in light your eyes cannot see.

goals.title: Apply the inverse-square law
goals.description: Student can use the inverse-square law to compute how the apparent brightness of a source changes when its distance changes.
goals.hook: Tell how far away a light is from how bright it looks.

goals.title: Explain why aperture matters
goals.description: Student can explain why a telescope's light-gathering power grows with the square of its aperture and how aperture limits the finest detail it can resolve.
goals.hook: Know what actually makes one telescope better than another.

goals.title: Compute a star's distance from parallax
goals.description: Student can compute a star's distance in parsecs from its parallax angle in arcseconds, and explain why parallax only works for nearby stars.
goals.hook: Measure the distance to a star with geometry alone.

goals.title: Compare stars on the magnitude scale
goals.description: Student can compare the brightness of two stars from their magnitudes, remembering that the scale runs backwards and that 5 magnitudes is a factor of 100.
goals.hook: Decode the strange scale astronomers use for brightness.

goals.title: Read a star's spectral class
goals.description: Student can order the spectral classes O B A F G K M by surface temperature and color, and place the Sun among them.
goals.hook: Know a star's temperature from its color.

goals.title: Place stars on the H-R diagram
goals.description: Student can place a star on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram from its temperature and luminosity, and name the main sequence, giants and white dwarfs.
goals.hook: Read the one chart that organizes every star.

goals.title: Explain fusion on the main sequence
goals.description: Student can explain how hydrogen fusion in the core powers a main-sequence star and why more massive stars burn out faster.
goals.hook: Understand why the Sun shines and how long it will.

goals.title: Predict a star's end state from its mass
goals.description: Student can predict whether a star ends as a white dwarf, a neutron star or a black hole from its initial mass.
goals.hook: Know how the Sun will die, and how the giants do.

goals.title: Describe the Milky Way's structure
goals.description: Student can describe the Milky Way's disk, bulge and halo, where the Sun sits in it, and why we see the galaxy as a band across the sky.
goals.hook: Know your address in the galaxy.

goals.title: Classify galaxies by shape
goals.description: Student can classify a galaxy as spiral, elliptical or irregular from an image and relate each type to its stars and gas.
goals.hook: Sort the galaxies in any deep-sky photograph.

goals.title: Explain the rotation-curve evidence for dark matter
goals.description: Student can explain why flat galaxy rotation curves imply more mass than the visible stars and gas, and what that unseen mass is called.
goals.hook: See the evidence for matter no one has ever seen.

goals.title: Explain cosmological redshift
goals.description: Student can explain redshift as the stretching of light's wavelength and compute a redshift from an observed and a rest wavelength.
goals.hook: Read a galaxy's motion from the color of its light.

goals.title: Use Hubble's law to estimate a distance
goals.description: Student can use Hubble's law (velocity equals the Hubble constant times distance) to estimate a galaxy's distance from its recession velocity.
goals.hook: Measure the size of the universe with one equation.

goals.title: List the evidence for the Big Bang
goals.description: Student can list the main evidence for the Big Bang (the expansion, the cosmic microwave background, the abundance of light elements) and say what each shows.
goals.hook: Know why astronomers are confident the universe had a beginning.
